# Onboarding: your first hour with this kit

This copy is for OpenCode. Type `/onboard` there and your agent shows it one step at a time; you can also read it all here.

## Step 1 of 7: Who this is for

People who want to use an AI coding agent on real projects, including people
who have never used one. The kit you installed gives you standing rules (in
`~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`), three helper agents, a few commands and a commit check. This
walkthrough adds a first hour of practice on your own code.

It comes one step at a time. Each step ends with the command for the next one,
so you can stop whenever you like and pick up later. Ask your agent about
anything that is unclear, right there; that is usually faster than searching
the docs.

Next: type `/onboard 2` to go on.

## Step 2 of 7: Your plan

In OpenCode you connect one or more providers, and each one bills its own way.
Type `/connect` to add one, and `/models` to see the models your connected
providers offer. A model is named `provider/model`, for example
`anthropic/<model>`. Find the providers you use:

- **OpenAI, signed in with ChatGPT Plus or Pro** (provider `openai`): a usage limit that resets; no command in the tool shows how much is left. Whether you can pay past the limit is unconfirmed; plan on waiting for the reset.
- **OpenAI, with an API key** (provider `openai`): billed per token; `opencode stats` shows what you spent.
- **Anthropic, with an API key** (provider `anthropic`): billed per token; `opencode stats` shows what you spent.
- **OpenRouter** (provider `openrouter`): billed per token; `opencode stats` shows what you spent.
- **A local model through Ollama** (provider `ollama`): runs on your own machine, free per token.

On a plan with a usage limit, stay on the starter tier, and use the `verifier`
agent on work that matters rather than on every edit. On an API key you pay for
every token: starter is still the place to start, and `opencode stats` in a
terminal shows what you have spent. A small local model may print its tool
calls as text instead of running them; if that happens, use a hosted model for
the kit's agents.

You chose the tier when you installed. To change it, run the installer again
with the other tier; `--dry-run` shows the plan and changes nothing:
- bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/install.py --tool opencode --tier full --dry-run`
- PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\install.py" --tool opencode --tier full --dry-run`

Next: type `/onboard 3` to go on.

## Step 3 of 7: The 5-minute mental model

Skip this if you have used OpenCode for a while; it is here as reference.

**Sessions.** Each time you run `opencode` in a folder, you start a session: a
conversation with that folder as its workspace. The agent can read files there
and, as your permissions allow, edit them and run commands. `/new` starts a
fresh session, `/sessions` switches between them, and `opencode --continue`
picks up the last one.

**AGENTS.md.** A plain text file of standing instructions OpenCode reads at the
start of every session. `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` applies to all your
projects; an `AGENTS.md` in a repo applies to that repo. `/init` writes a first
draft of one for a repo by reading it. This is where house rules go.

**Agents.** `Tab` switches between the Build agent, which makes changes, and
the Plan agent, which is restricted to researching and proposing. The kit adds
three subagents: `verifier`, `code-reviewer` and `consultant`. Type
`@verifier` (or ask for the verifier agent) to send one off on a job; it works
in its own context and reports back.

**Permissions.** The `permission` setting in `opencode.json` decides, per tool,
whether the agent may go ahead (`allow`), must ask you first (`ask`) or may
never (`deny`). The kit added `allow` rules only for a few read-only git
commands. Its subagents are denied editing.

**Commands.** Typed shortcuts that run a saved prompt. OpenCode's own include
`/init`, `/new`, `/compact`, `/models`, `/connect` and `/undo`. The kit's are
`/checkpoint`, `/lanes`, `/onboard` and `/starter-update`.

**Skills.** Checklists the agent loads only when the work matches, such as the
kit's backend and frontend guardrails. `opencode debug skill` lists them.

**Context and compaction.** Everything in the session (your messages, files
read, command output) shares one context window. When it fills, OpenCode
summarises older parts. Run `/compact` yourself at a natural break, or `/new`
when switching to an unrelated task, so stale detail does not crowd out what
matters now. `/undo` takes back the last message and the file changes it made.

**Usage.** Long sessions, large files, bigger models and many subagents all
spend faster, on a plan's limit or on your API bill.

Next: type `/onboard 4` to go on.

## Step 4 of 7: How this kit works

The rules ask your agent to work like this:

- **Classify the task first:** say whether it is a spike, a change to something
  that exists, or new architecture, because each needs a different amount of
  care.
- **Root cause before fix:** a fix for a bug you do not understand is a guess,
  and three failed fixes means the design is wrong.
- **Verify independently:** the agent that did the work does not get to declare
  it done; another one re-runs the checks.
- **Say what you ran versus what you reasoned:** "tests pass" means they ran and
  someone read the output, and commits record which is which.
- **Simplest thing first:** no new dependency or service without evidence it is
  needed, built so the bigger option can replace it later.
- **Confirm before anything outward-facing:** pushes, deploys, messages and
  deletes wait for your yes, because git cannot undo them.

Each rule is written down with the reason it exists, in `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`.
Keep a rule only while you can say what failure it prevents.

Next: type `/onboard 5` to go on.

## Step 5 of 7: What you got

The installer wrote the kit's rules into `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, inside
a block marked `BEGIN claude-starter rules`, and added the agents, commands and
skills below. It backed up every file it changed.

| Piece | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `/checkpoint` | After a change: runs the relevant checks, says what ran and what did not, proposes a commit message, waits for your yes |
| `verifier` agent | Re-runs build and tests on work reported as done, without editing anything |
| `code-reviewer` agent | Reviews a diff for the ways this project breaks (money, auth, time, data), not style |
| `consultant` agent | Answers a question about another part of the codebase so your session does not have to read it all |
| `/lanes` | Splits a repo with several stacks (say, a frontend and a backend) into lanes |
| `/starter-update` | Updates the kit: shows the plan, applies nothing until you say yes |
| Guardrail skills | Checks while writing endpoints, UI, data jobs and code that calls a model |
| Commit guard | In repos you gave the installer with `--guard-repo`: checks commits for secrets, personal data and a `Verified:` or `Unverified:` line |

To check it all loaded, run `opencode agent list` in a terminal and look for
the three agents. To add the commit guard to a repo, run the installer again
with `--guard-repo` (use the tier you installed; `--dry-run` changes nothing):
- bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/install.py --tool opencode --tier starter --guard-repo <your-repo> --dry-run`
- PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\install.py" --tool opencode --tier starter --guard-repo <your-repo> --dry-run`

Next: type `/onboard 6` to go on.

## Step 6 of 7: Your first hour

Do this in a repo of your own with a clean `git status`. Make a branch first so
nothing lands on your main branch by accident.

1. **Open it.** `cd` into the repo and run `opencode`.
2. **Run `/init`.** Read the `AGENTS.md` it writes. Correct anything wrong: how
   to run the tests, what the project is, what must never break. This file is
   worth more than any prompt you will type.
3. **Ask for a small change.** Pick something real and small: a confusing
   function to tidy, a missing test, a bug you already understand. Notice that
   the agent says how it classifies the task before it starts. If it guesses
   wrong, say so. Press `Tab` first if you want the Plan agent to propose
   before anything changes.
4. **Run `/checkpoint`.** It runs the checks that cover the change, tells you
   what it did not run, shows the diff and proposes a commit message with a
   `Verified:` or `Unverified:` line. It stops and waits for you.
5. **Ask for an independent check.** Type something like: "@verifier check that
   this change works." Compare its report with what the session claimed. Any
   gap between the two is the point of the exercise.
6. **Commit, if you are happy.** Approve the commit. Where the commit guard is
   installed, read any warning it gives and decide whether it is real. If the
   change went wrong instead, `/undo` takes it back.

Next: type `/onboard 7` to go on.

## Step 7 of 7: Where to go next

- **Graduate to full:** once you regularly run several agents at once, install
  the full tier. It adds rules for picking a model and effort level per task
  and for coordinating agents. `--dry-run` shows the plan first; restart
  OpenCode after the install:
  - bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/install.py --tool opencode --tier full --dry-run`
  - PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\install.py" --tool opencode --tier full --dry-run`
- **Pin a model to an agent:** the kit's agents run on the session's model. To
  pin one, add `model: provider/model` to its file in
  `~/.config/opencode/agents/`. `MODELS.md` in the kit says which role each
  agent plays.
- **A repo with two stacks:** run `/lanes` once in it.
- **Make the rules yours:** edit `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, outside the
  block marked `BEGIN claude-starter rules`; an update replaces that block.
  Keep a rule only while you can say what failure it prevents.
- **Keep it current:** `/starter-update` shows what a new release changes and
  applies nothing until you say yes.
- **Something misbehaved:** if the commit guard flags something it should not,
  or an agent or skill from this kit does something wrong, run this in a
  terminal. It saves a redacted report and sends nothing unless you add
  `--submit` and confirm (`--kind` can also be `agent-misbehaved`):
  - bash: `python ~/.claude-starter/scripts/report.py --kind guard-false-positive --tool opencode --step "what happened"`
  - PowerShell: `python "$HOME\.claude-starter\scripts\report.py" --kind guard-false-positive --tool opencode --step "what happened"`

That was the last step. Next: after your next change, type `/checkpoint`.
